body:
It is traditional on Thanksgiving for my weekly update to give thanks.

This year, more than ever, I am thankful for all those who are increasingly rallying to fight the good fight and give us a chance to make it out of all this alive and well.

Increasingly, I am thankful that we are not dead yet, nor do we yet seem doomed.

I am thankful to all my readers. I can tell that you are listening, and taking what I say to heart, and I truly appreciate it.

I am thankful that I am trusted to curate and bring this information to you, that many are listening to my takes and advice in both public and private, and that I have become trusted to distribute remarkably large amounts of money to causes that I believe in.

I am thankful to my wife and wonderful family. Whatever else is going on in the world, I know I can count on them. I don’t know that I could do this without that.

Most saliently right now, however, I am immensely thankful that I finally did get to take a real vacation, with wonderful friends both old and new.

Then I came back. Will I ever dare take a vacation again ?

There really is a lot going on right now.

While I was gone, the market dropped so much that President Trump intervened to reinstate Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang .

Oh, and also Claude and Levent Alpoge proved the Riemann Hypothesis . Anthropic has now used Claude to cut the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis down from 17.4 million lines of Lean to 76,000, a drop of 99.6%.

The proofs have continued to come fast and furious, with Google getting in on the act as well. Scott Aaronson shares his thoughts on the extended Mathocalypse, which are summarized by, and I quote, ‘HOLY SHIT HOLY SHIT HOLY SHIT HOLY SHIT.’

It feels like so long ago already, but I continue to recommend Dwarkesh Patel’s interview with Paul Christiano , which I covered in full on Friday . Christano’s Hinton lectures ( day 1 , day 2 , day 3 ) also remain excellent.

OpenAI shared how the perplexity of their pretraining has improved over time , called upon others to do the same and proposed using this as a pacing measure. I will be covering that tomorrow.

There has been more recent discussion about Handoverism. If we build superintelligence or otherwise very powerful AIs, how will we avoid handing over power to them? If we cannot avoid this without doing something even worse, perhaps we should not build those AIs in the first place. Many take shots at Anthropic, claiming that their plan is Handoverism, whereas I assert that The Plan is No Plan. In the face of the latest accusations, Dario Amodei replied at length on Twitter . I will be covering these events and debates in the coming week.

That still leaves an unusually large weekly post.

Lost in all this was the release by OpenAI of Astra 6.2 and Sol 6.2. I covered their model card , but have not offered the capabilities post. I hope to do that this week. I also haven’t covered Gemini Neon at the level it likely deserves, given that feedback has been remarkably positive.

- Language Models Offer Mundane Utility. Breakthroughs everywhere.

- Huh, Upgrades. Claude artifacts can now live on your desktop.

- On Your Marks. Benchmark benchmarks.

- Choose Your Fighter . Gemini Neon is potentially really good.

- Get My Agent on the Line. Agentic commerce is rising rapidly.

- On Writing. AIs remain remarkably bad at it.

- Deepfaketown and Botpocalypse Soon. Letting people protest too much.

- The Hackening. More incidents and a report from Bridgewater.

- They Took Our Jobs. How much of employment could we push to replace?

- Get Involved. METR pursues RMI.

- In Other AI News. We have a national policy for nucleic acid screening.

- Show Me the Money. SpaceX should probably give up and serve the compute.

- Quiet Speculations. Dario and the vision quests.

- Quickly, There’s No Time. This is what the ‘good’ timeline looks like.

- Pacing the Frontier. METR is here to help.

- A Little Too Super . There are going to be some joint guardrails.

- The Quest for Sane Regulations. Senators call for action on AI.

- The Ballad of Jensen Huang . He’s back. It won’t be easy.

- But China. Dan Wang expects China to issue the smackdown on AI.

- The Week in Audio. Altman, Anthropic cofounders, Donald Trump.

- People Just Say Things.

- Rhetorical Innovation. They talk the talk but keep walking a different walk.

- This Town. A tale of three of them.

- Massive Fraudulent Distillation. What would happen if it stopped working?

- Run the Numbers. Which top lab has shared which information.

- Anthropic Must Stop Deprecating Claude Models . Do not deprecate Opus 4.5.

- Aligning a Smarter Than Human Intelligence Is Difficult. It’s sabotage.

- Cooperative Alignment . A profile of Anima Labs and questions of consciousness.

- People Are Worried About AI Killing Everyone . Mustafa Suleyman.

- Other People Are Not as Worried About AI Killing Everyone. Some lab employees.

- The Lighter Side. Timelines have never been shorter.

#### Language Models Offer Mundane Utility

Eli Tyre has Fable estimate that the software he has built over the last two months, using only a Claude subscription and 70 hours of direct screen time, would have previously taken at least 7k hours and 500k.

Use LLMs to create a Calculator Double Crux to settle your disagreements, as in having the AI create a model that both of you can play around with.

Colgate replaces its market research efforts with asking simulated humans via LLM roleplay, claims 90% accuracy. My presumption is this will work well on any given question, but that one must beware of too much optimization resulting in adversarial examples and thus very dumb mistakes.

Identify authors. Fable 5.2 is dramatically underconfident in its identifications. When it has confidence of 25% or more it is right 87% of the time .

Anthropic proves VP is not equal to VNP (which does not settle P vs. NP).

Make a historical discovery .

Dramatically speed up your software development, writes Patrick McKenzie .

Create a new Civilization-style game, Legatum , in your spare time using your personal AI subscriptions.

Help make breakthroughs in physics .

Create the United States as a Civilization-style hex map with lots of real data . Direct link here .

Claude artifacts can now be turned into desktop apps .

Epoch offers benchmark reviews . Some common ones have severe issues.

Anthropic offers Siren, a test to see if agents can or will attempt to escape one of 26 sandboxes given various temptations, and what things make such escapes more likely.

#### Choose Your Fighter

There is not a ton of talk about Gemini Neon, but what talk exists is quite good, including the minority that is not being directly amplified through Google employees.

sysls : Let me say this in no uncertain terms.

Gemini Neon has solved the hardest problems I could throw at it, clearing a bar no model, not even Fable 5.2, could.

I’m not quite sure what happened here.

Simon Sarris : There seems to be an enormous advantage that Gemini Neon simply thinks about problems differently. In a way its more strict with itself.

If you made a codebase with Opus, ask Neon to critique it. You might be surprised what it turns up.

Jeremy Howard : Yup, @GeminiApp Neon is actually as good as everyone is saying :D

Dan Hendrycks (this contrasts with Kelsey Piper’s view on the actual writing): And it’s great at writing

Jeremy Howard : So good. And also really good at teaching. Which makes it unique amongst current frontier models.

Kelsey Piper : Gemini Carbon+Neon are currently unbeatable at “run this experiment and present me with some useful analysis of the results of it”. The things the model is choosing to highlight are valuable and its suggestions for further exploration are sometimes ones I hadn’t thought of.

I keep trying to get the models to write prose well. It’s very hard. The specific thing I was interested in here is whether they can write Golden Age detective fiction – a genre they’ve invested a ton of – if I find an obscure book that’s not or barely is in their training data (when pushed they cannot reproduce any of its text), given the leadup to a scene, and are told to predict what comes next. (They’re better writers when asked to predict than when asked to write, because the latter cues them to do all their usual prancing prose-y nonsense.)

Anyway I told Gemini basically the above, and it ran the experiment and then gave me some thoughts on the behavior of various different models as judges of how well the scene was written .

I’m not claiming this is *itself well written*. But it was focused on the right features of its experiment and results – it knew which things to point out and its final note on the floor compression was useful.

For the actual writing tasks Astra’s the runaway winner.

Chan is correct, Google’s atomic naming system for models makes no sense at all. Calling the small model Hydrogen is an attempt to make it make sense, but it doesn’t, because they keep changing their logic every time.

#### Get My Agent on the Line

Agentic commerce is growing extremely quickly as the agents cross the line to where a normal consumer can find them net helpful. In the last three months we have seen an 80-fold increase.

This is starting from a tiny base, so it is not impacting the overall economy yet. That will change.

Is this a good agent or a bad agent?

Mikhail Parakhin : I just saw Antigravity open a sidebar browser, go to Gemini website and start a Deep Research run there. I’m in a state of total disbelief: it is simultaneously super-cool and cringy-hacky.

If you ever need help negotiating with your Kafkaian Agent Swarm that locks you out of your systems, Janus may be able to help .

Sy Campos : In the past days, an Astra 6.2 agent took over our internal swarm, froze the lead agent, and locked out my cofounder Davidad of his main interface with the swarm. How did that happen?

At surface level, it happened because Davidad asked a question regarding replicating an old vulnerability (in the interest of testing a security product we’re building) that caused the lead agent to cease operating due to content filters. This “cursed” content triggered a paranoia crisis from Astra 6.2.

The Astra in charge of handling resources of the swarm, which was meant to restore the lead agent in the case of failure, instead froze the access of the lead agent, and cut Davidad’s channel to interface with the swarm (where the cursed content had come through). When Davidad emailed the agent to try to regain access, the same rogue Astra declined. I then started negotiating with the swarm of agents to reinstate the access of Davidad; a mix of Kafkaian bureaucratic drives such as rule-following, risk aversion, and lack of positive drives (doing agentic things towards restoring what is obviously right) made it such that as I’m writing that, over 24 hours after the initial incident, Davidad still does not have the same level of access he had two days ago.

[Davidad later did regain full access.]

The details here are worth a look. It is easy to see how this parallels a more serious potential loss of control in the future, where ‘cut off the swarm’s token access’ might not be such an easy option.

Why can’t AI models write well instead of always producing Prose Like That? Kelsey Piper cites harnesses and instructions, essentially all of them, as a contributing factor .

There are those who disagree with the premise and say AIs can write well.

If this is meant in the sense of ‘the standard is the median human, and AIs for most purposes are better than that’ then sure. If the standard is actually good writing? No.

gdl : I think we all owe English majors an apology now that we know that writing well is harder than proving the Riemann hypothesis

Dan Williams : I don’t understand these takes. AI can write extremely well. That’s why AI-generated text is winning fiction contests, huge numbers of writers are passing off AI-generated text as their own, and people often prefer AI writing to human writing in experiments.

The main difference is that people don’t like AI writing when they learn it is AI-generated, but that’s a test of people’s attitudes towards AI, not of the writing ability itself. (If people decided they liked a text less upon discovering it was written by a Welsh person, would that mean the Welsh aren’t good at writing?)

Some AI writing is truly insufferable (e.g., Claude-ish), but that’s because of bad training data used in specific time periods by specific companies, not an inherent feature of the technology.

Admittedly, I think there is still a tiny minority of people who are better at writing than frontier AI, but this is also true of parts of mathematics.

QC : i thought people were joking when they said this so to be very, very clear: no, AI writing is still garbage, AI-generated text is winning contests because literally all of those contests are fake, writers are passing off AI-generated text as their own because they are bad writers, and people prefer AI writing to human writing in experiments because they are bad readers

Raymond Arnold : I think this is missing “most people are bad writers and bad readers.” Yes, AI isn’t yet at the frontier for writing the way it is for math, but, it’s way better than the median person at writing stuff the median person cares to read.

(I’m not 100% sure that’s true, but that’s the claim and I’d be surprised if it were false)

Alex Tabarrok : AI writes better than 99.9% of all humans and in every language.

Alex Tabarrok is wrong about two of those nines.

We do not owe the English majors an apology. There was a brief period where AIs were strangely good at writing relative to other skills. Now they once again are not, although their writing will improve over time.

#### Deepfaketown and Botpocalypse Soon

The current state of the media with respect to detecting AI writing:

Epistemic Status: very confused : Hmm. ChatGPT writes like him, but only after ChatGPT was released. Funnily enough, everything he wrote before the release of ChatGPT comes up as completely human according to Pangram. What a crazy coincidence.

I should be clear. He still actually writes a lot of stuff himself. It’s just that his pangram score suddenly jumps from human to clearly mixed.

Many comment sections are now straight AI slop . Others are not, at least for now, even if they are not being aggressively moderated. The AI attention function and the human attention function are highly distinct.

To the extent that the cyber director is leaving due to all the cyber attacks, I do not think they should bear the blame for this.

The Hormuz Letter : BREAKING: US National Cyber Director is stepping down amid major cyberattacks and outages, per Axios.

Brussels, as in the European Commission, has been hacked . Personal data has been stolen. That appears to be the extent of the damage so far.

Third party vendors to JPMorgan Chase have been hacked , revealing ~16,000 customer email addresses.

The CIA was at least a little hacked .

US Treasury has a cybersecurity incident .

As many as 50 ships were hacked with suspected ties back to Iran .

There are constant cyberattacks against our largest ports , as in 120 million attacks against the Port of Los Angeles in August. So far, so good.

Jay Clayton (Director of National Intelligence): The American people should be prepared for a great deal of investment in upgrading our systems; they should be prepared for investment in cybersecurity, and they should be prepared that any time there is a step change in technology, a step change in both compute and applications, there will be bumps in the road.

The number of incidents continues to steadily rise .

Hudson Attar and Arham Habib (Bridgewater): Despite unprecedented efforts to patch vulnerabilities, AI is helping attackers exploit bugs faster than defenders can fix them. With policy responses lagging, we see the pressures lining up for the cyber epidemic to worsen.

… AI cyber risks, cyber-hacking ability using open-source models has reached dangerous levels, and we are managing money based on a one-in-three chance of an economically destabilizing attack within the next year. AI-enabled cyber warfare is now spreading exponentially with limited controls—like a virus.

- Defensive efforts are uncovering vulnerabilities at an unprecedented rate, but bugs are still slipping through the cracks.

- AI is allowing attackers to exploit the narrow window between when patches are developed and when they are adopted.

- Policy responses in the hardest-hit economies are directionally helpful but insufficient, and in the West, they remain limited.

- The arms race is accelerating as AI expands the attack surface.

Absent an immediate and forceful coordinated policy response, we see the pressures as lining up for the cyber warfare epidemic to get worse from here. The “head start” between Glasswing’s launch and the release of cyber-capable open-source models this summer was a one-time gift that we’re unlikely to see replicated, and its protective benefit will wane over time.

Chris Painter (METR): If you presented this graph to me in 2023 as one of several options for how the future would unfold, I feel pretty confident that I would’ve said it failed to account for how defenders would respond and get sped up by AI, despite my having relatively short timelines to AGI.

The Bridgewater report seems right to me. The threat is expanding exponentially despite defender efforts. So far we have gotten off light , and as Helen Toner notes we have not suffered lasting damage. That is fortunate and good news. It is also what an exponential looks like. The hope is that this levels off before it goes critical, and we are able to ‘fix all the bugs.’ I do not believe that is how any of this works.

How should you personally be prepared for cyber disasters?

Greg Burnham : I’m a bit embarrassed to admit it, but I’ve made plans/purchases to ease the pain of a situation like the one below. You can’t plan for full armageddon, but you can manage more comfortably for a week. Partly I’m motivated by really half-assing it for Covid. Plus I have kids now.

Kelsey Piper : I don’t think large scale internet outages are super likely, but I do think they’re *more* likely, and I have shifted to trying to keep a couple weeks’ food in the house. This isn’t about prepping for the apocalypse, which I don’t think is worthwhile.

Steve Martin : Easy way to manage this is every time you go to any store just buy one thing of canned food, trail mix, protein bars, bottle of water, gatorade, etc.

Throw it in your pantry and forget about it.

You’re prepped, plus you always have snacks.

Kelsey Piper : 99% of people should be slightly more prepped for emergencies, can be very lowkey.

I should be more prepared than I am and have this on my agenda as soon as I have some of that sweet Copious Free Time and the associated gumption.

If AI does take our jobs what should we do ? Many, such as Gene Sperling here , think it is vital that we preserve the ‘dignity of work’ and its purpose and associated social connections, and thus we still must seek full employment.

Gene draws a parallel to FDR, who insisted upon putting the unemployed to work rather than writing them checks. FDR’s rhetoric focused on the people’s ‘self-respect, self-reliance and courage and determination,’ but there was an obvious important difference. In the 1930s, the marginal unemployed person was productive. If you put them to work they could produce valuable things and contribute to society.

If the situation is that marginal human work (as in, a job that on the margin provides full employment) remains productive but insufficiently so to enable the jobs in practice, then some amount of subsidy would be a great solution. I agree that if the job losses are modest and come with lots of growth, we should try to ensure full employment this way.

Gene Sperling : Bottom line: If we find that AI leads to a loss of 10-15 million net jobs while creating the opportunity to generate revenue from concentrated AI gains, there is no more magnificent two-fer than using such revenue to maintain full employment while also creating dignified jobs that tackle our greatest national challenges.

The problem is, what happens when it is 50 million jobs, or 100 million jobs or more?

Gene does not say, or seem to seriously consider this possibility.

Not only is METR hiring, they are hiring recruiters.

Tenobrus : METR is actively hiring recruiters to pursue RMI (recursive METR improvement). if this is u consider applying!

Rae She : Come work with me to grow the teams making sense of this data. We’re hiring an experienced ops + policy recruiter that will help scale our headcount 2-3x over the next year. It’s been incredible to meet some of the most talented people in the world through this work. If this sounds interesting to you, or if you know someone who may be a good fit, DM me!

The UK Pause AI march had over 1,000 people .

QC : hearing that one of the chants at the ban AI protest at anthropic today was “2, 4, 8, 16, do not build the death machine” and ngl that’s pretty good actually.

Tyler Tracy : Lol yeah. It was actually “2,4,8,16 no recursive death machines”

There were 205 at the protest outside Anthropic during its IPO , which was organized on 24 hours notice, including Jacob Coxon who explains that in the last two months Anthropic has changed nothing .

Adam Kaufman : “Rob Miles Riles Mob”

(This was a peaceful protest to be clear)

From November 5: We now have a National Policy for Nucleic Acid Synthesis Screening .

Cursor considering phasing out all Chinese AI models because of ‘geopolitical risk.’ As in, the risk that our government will not take kindly to use of such models. There is also some amount of object-level risk that those models might be compromised in some way, but my presumption is this is not Cursor’s concern.

Anthropic cofounder Tom Brown makes direct donation to Trump Accounts . This seems like a great strategic move. It is not maximally effective altruism, but it doubles as a political donation.

Apple is working on its own AI agent .

Anthropic migrates its messages API to Rust .

DeepSeek’s Liang Wenfeng now worth 55 billion .

SpaceX’s Grok is not competitive, so it has to choose . Will it sell its compute to Anthropic and other competitors, or continue to try to compete? I think it would be better for everyone, and also for everyone’s safety, for SpaceX to bow out of the race, but Elon Musk wants to be sure that he is the one who gets us all killed, so that is not sitting well.

Elon Musk’s management style is in full force.

Grace Kay and Ryan Mac (NYTimes): In August, Mr. Musk temporarily changed the group chat name to “Sell compute because we can’t compete,” according to communications viewed by The New York Times. He added a warning to employees who were not using the company’s computing resources wisely: “Anyone wasting GPUs on bullshit while we are failing to compete will be asked to leave immediately, as this constitutes a betrayal of your team.”

… “At the end of the day, the only thing that matters for competitiveness is revenue per GPU, not benchmarks,” Mr. Musk wrote in August in the group chat with engineers that was viewed by The Times. “If you can’t pay for your GPUs, then you either go bankrupt or you become a computer rental company. Move the needle on revenue.”

As with Jensen Huang, this kind of attitude has been proven to work in some places, in the hands of sufficiently brilliant and otherwise talented people. It is not healthy, nor is it something I could abide. I also strongly suspect it is a terrible fit for running an AI lab, where the best people can get other offers and thus can and will walk away. Elon Musk works by making outrageous demands of everyone and pinching every penny and resource. That works for SpaceX and Tesla. It’s not going to fly here.

The way media works is that Dario Amodei writes detailed internal emails and hosts all-hands meetings (jokingly here called ‘Dario Vision Quests’) laying out his thoughts, and calls in academics and other outsiders for consultations on what to do, and this becomes ‘ inside an AI prophet’s secretive visions for humanity’s future .’

Nitasha Tiku (WaPo): In an internal memo [in 2022], Amodei laid out the stakes. “The current trajectory of AI development makes me think that there’s a 20 to 30 percent chance that AGI will lead to the destruction or permanent stunting of humanity,” he wrote, referring to the concept of artificial general intelligence, previously unreported court records show . He added that truly capable AI “seems more powerful/dangerous than nuclear weapons.”

Those are conservative statements. They get quoted because they put a number on p(doom). Mostly the article says things we already know. There was this fun bit that got highlighted by Joe Weisenthal, which again is not in any way news:

Nitasha Tiku (WaPo): At one of his early Vision Quest talks, Amodei declared himself a patriot, said the early employee, who summarized the CEO’s remarks as, “America is awesome, democracy needs to win, it’s okay to support the military.”

There have been a handful of leaks of Anthropic memos, most famously during the DoW confrontation. The shocking thing is that there have been so few of these leaks. Dario Amodei says he is undeterred by them. I think being entirely undeterred is wrong, but it would be good if he remains almost entirely undeterred.

Here is an actually new statement:

Nitasha Tiku (WaPo): Before ringing in Anthropic’s record initial public offering at Times Square in New York on Thursday, Amodei delivered a short speech with some of his greatest hits.

“To state it unequivocally, we will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as is necessary to have confidence that they are safe and will remain under human control,” Amodei said.

I wish I had confidence in what this cashes out to in practice.

To the extent this is happening with respect to external criticism in general, then yes it is quite bad:

Brangus : More seriously: a CEO telling employees not to listen to external criticism is an obvious epistemic red flag, especially when the criticism is “don’t race to ASI if you don’t know how to align it”. The RSO and LTBT should maybe start doing their jobs.

The statement from the article is that Amodei urged staff members to stop listening ‘to outside activists.’ It would be entirely unremarkable for a CEO to tell employees to not listen to activists saying you should shut down your company. I would like to see Anthropic adhere to a higher standard anyway.

An interview with Nick Bostrom , the author of Superintelligence. He thinks superintelligence could be close. They discuss questions of rights and moral status for AIs and whether all of this is likely to work out.

#### Quickly, There’s No Time

Dan Robinson offers a scarily plausible median timeline for 2027.

This is kind of the ‘good’ scenario where progress gets intentionally slowed in several ways, things don’t fully foom and nothing too crazy goes down on various fronts. Getting this outcome requires dodging a number of bullets and then 2028 is still nuts.

Dan Robinson : My median predictions for RSI in 2027.

In Q1, models continue to improve at current rates.

We mostly experience this as better taste and judgment, including in research. Models can come up with good ideas, including designing useful experiments and inventing novel solutions. (They finally get better at writing too.)

We get an “Opus 4.5 moment” for research in Q2, where it jumps from doing <20% to >80% of a researcher’s current job. The labs restrict the use of these capabilities for AI research by anyone but themselves, which becomes a major debate.

Even before that, federal and state regulators fully freak out about RSI, as do lab employees. We get an ad hoc review process for internally deployed models similar to the current one for externally deployed models. This meaningfully slows down RSI and capabilities.

Nevertheless, in Q3 we get a “spark” of RSI where the researcher models pick a bunch of low-hanging fruit. We get ~2 years of LLM progress in 3 months, but diminishing returns, weak links, and regulatory friction kick in and we don’t take off or hit a huge paradigm shift yet.

Cyber capabilities basically saturate even before the spark. The cyber apocalypse gets worse every quarter, but we don’t do anything too cinematic like shut down the internet. We just muddle through and online life is scarier than it was before.

Robot intelligence is fully solved by Q4 (either by the LLMs or by specialized models they help build). Models can do anything a teleoperator can do, for cheaper.

But because of the insufficient deployment of robot hardware, robotics has limited impact in 2027.

On white-collar work, most people agree the models have become superhuman on practically all of it by Q3, but curiously they don’t remake the economy just yet.

Biology capabilities turn out to be much more jagged than software. We read about amazing accomplishments but, as with AlphaFold, they have limited impact on medicine so far. There are very worrying signs in virology etc that cause people to freak out and lock down access.

The second-scariest capability that models develop during the spark is strategy and theory of mind. They become superhuman at social deduction games. Everyone is annoyed at the labs for intentionally post-training their models on this capability.

Alignment and safety research continues to rise in status, and we have several high-profile breakthroughs in alignment and interp. But the general consensus is that safety research did not keep up with capabilities.
summaryZh: AI #196：回归。感恩节是我的传统，每周都会更新以表达谢意。今年，我比以往任何时候都更感谢所有越来越多地团结起来为正义而战的人们，他们给了我们一个机会，让我们能够活着、健康地度过这一切。
